schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_kalmas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kalmas sands (within the Aral Karakum) are recorded in 19th-century Russian geographical and ethnographic accounts (e.g., 1834 wintering records of Kazakh Shomekei clans).

morphemes.translation: unremaining / impassable (negative aorist participle of qal- 'to remain')

b_kalmas.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh toponym Qalmas (Russian Kalmas), a sandy tract in the Aral Karakum northeast of the Aral Sea, derived from the Turkic verbal stem qal- ('to remain, stay') with the negative aorist suffix -mas.

b_arys-kum.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Aryskum sand desert in the Kyzylorda/Aral Karakum region is first documented in modern Russian Imperial and Soviet cartography.
b_arys-kum.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound Arysqum (Russian Aryskum), combining arys with qum ('sand, sandy desert'), designating a desert tract north of the lower Syr Darya.

b_chalkar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the settlement of Shalkar (formerly Chelkar) was founded in 1870 CE and granted town status in 1928 CE.
b_chalkar.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Shalqar (Russianized as Chelkar/Chalkar), meaning 'vast, boundless', referring to Lake Shalkar adjacent to the town in Aktobe Region.

b_chubar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Shubar (Chubar) is a modern Kazakh toponym documented only in post-medieval/modern cartography.
b_chubar.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh shubar (Russian Chubar), meaning 'speckled, dappled, variegated', a common descriptive element in Kazakh steppe toponymy.

b_terekli.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Terekli is a Turkic toponym documented in the Aral-Turgay region only in modern Russian Imperial/Soviet maps.
b_terekli.etymology_analysis: Turkic topographic descriptor terek-li ('abounding in poplars'), corresponding to Kazakh Terekti.

b_irgis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Irgiz River is tentatively identified with the 'Arkhaz' mentioned in Ibn Fadlan's 921-922 CE Risala, while the modern settlement of Yrgyz was founded in 1845 CE as a Russian fort.
b_irgis.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Yrghyz (Russian Irgiz), the name of a major right tributary of the Turgay River and the 1845 settlement on its banks; folk and linguistic etymologies link it to Turkic yrghy- ('to leap, jump') or a pre-Kazakh steppe hydronym.

b_airyuk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Airyk (Airyuk) in Aktobe Region is documented only in modern Russian Imperial and Soviet sources.
b_airyuk.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh ayryq / ayyryq (Russian Airyuk/Airyk), meaning 'fork, branch, division' (of a river or valley), a generic topographic descriptor.

b_jelavi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Jelavi' does not correspond to a documented pre-867 settlement and appears to be a synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name.

morphemes.translation: unidentified or synthetic CK3 place name (unknown etymology)

b_jelavi.etymology_analysis: Unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Barsuki/Aral region without a clear attested Kazakh or Russian cartographic counterpart.

b_barsuki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Greater and Lesser Barsuki deserts are first documented in modern Russian geographical surveys.
b_barsuki.etymology_analysis: Russianized form Barsuki of Kazakh Borsyq (Ülken Borsyq and Kishi Borsyq), derived from Turkic borsyq ('badger'), designating the twin sandy deserts north of the Aral Sea.

b_chushka-kol.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Shoshkakol (Chushka-Kol) in Aktobe Region is first documented in modern Russian/Soviet cartography.
b_chushka-kol.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Shoshqaköl (Russian Chushka-Kul / Shoshkakol), from shoshqa ('boar/pig') + köl ('lake').

b_jamantau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mount Zhamantau (Jamantau) in the southern Mugodzhar Hills is documented only in modern Russian/Kazakh cartography.
b_jamantau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Zhamantau (also Jamantau/Yamantau), from zhaman ('bad, barren') + tau ('mountain'), designating a 372 m massif at the southern end of the Mugodzhar Hills.

b_emba.first_mention_attestation: Earliest attestation of the form Emba appears in 1570 CE Russian diplomatic dispatches (Afanasy Nagoy's report on the Battle of Emba); earlier 6th-century Greek sources (Menander Protector, c. 584 CE) record the river under the older Turkic form Ikh (Ich).

morphemes.translation: river name (Emba, also known in Kazakh as Zhem)

b_emba.etymology_analysis: Russian Emba (Kazakh Embı or Zhem), a major river in western Kazakhstan flowing from the Mugodzhar Hills to the Caspian Sea; the Kazakh name Zhem reflects an older Turkic hydronym attested in Greek as Ich (Ikh) in the 6th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Menander Protector, History (recording Zemarchus's 569-571 CE journey)
older_name_by_867.notes: Menander Protector records the river crossed before the Daikh (Ural) and Attila (Volga) as the Ikh (Greek Ich), identified by historians with the Emba.

b_achu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Achu (Kazakh Ashchy) is a generic Turkic topographic name documented only in modern cartography.
b_achu.etymology_analysis: From Turkic/Kazakh ashchy / achu ('bitter, brackish, saline'), a common generic descriptor for brackish lakes, springs, and depressions in the Kazakh steppe.

current_repo_state.name: Atschu
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Atschu).

b_kyzyl_cheku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kyzyl-Cheku (Kazakh Qyzylshoqy) is a modern Kazakh topographic name documented only in 19th/20th-century cartography.
b_kyzyl_cheku.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Qyzylshoqy (Russianized as Kyzyl-Cheku), a descriptive compound from qyzyl ('red') + shoqy ('peak, hillock').

b_jilali.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Jilali is a minor Kazakh steppe toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_jilali.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym (Zhylaly / Jilali), likely derived from Turkic zhyla- ('to weep, trickle') or a dialectal/cartographic variant of zhylandy ('snaky') with the adjectival suffix -ly.

current_repo_state.name: Jilali
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Jilali).

b_janai_cheku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Janai-Cheku (Kazakh Zhanayshoqy) is a modern Kazakh hill toponym unattested before modern cartography.
b_janai_cheku.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Zhanayshoqy (Russianized as Janai-Cheku), a compound of the Kazakh name Zhanay and shoqy ('peak, hillock').

b_ulu_jitanjik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Uly-Zhylanshyk (Ulu-Jilanchik) River is documented only in modern Russian Imperial and Soviet geographical surveys.
b_ulu_jitanjik.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Uly-Zhylanshyq (CK3 spelling Ulu Jitanjik, Russian Ulu-Dzhilanchik), a qualifier compound meaning 'Great Zhylanshyk', from uly ('great') + zhylan ('snake') + diminutive -shyq.

b_karalbak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Karalbak' has no documented pre-867 attestation and appears to be a synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name.
b_karalbak.etymology_analysis: Unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Turgay/Kokturgay region, likely incorporating Turkic qara ('black') with an obscure or garbled second element.

b_sor_kuduk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sor-Kuduk (Kazakh Sorqudyq) is a generic Kazakh well toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_sor_kuduk.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Sorqudyq (Russian Sorkuduk), a generic common-noun compound from sor ('salt marsh, solonchak') + qudyq ('well').

b_eghiz_kala.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Egizkara (CK3: Eghiz Kala / Eghiz Kara) is a Kazakh topographic name documented only in modern cartography.

morphemes.translation: black / dark (or qala 'fort/town' in the barony key)

b_eghiz_kala.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Egizqara ('Twin Black [hills/elevations]'), from egiz ('twin') + qara ('black'); the CK3 barony key b_eghiz_kala substitutes qala ('fort/town') for qara.

b_terekti.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Terekti is a common Kazakh topographic name documented only in modern cartography.
b_terekti.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Terekti ('poplar-grove / place with poplars'), from terek ('poplar') + adjectival suffix -ti.

b_kara_sor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Karasor (Kazakh Qarasor) is a common Kazakh salt-lake toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_kara_sor.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Qarasor (Russian Karasor), from qara ('black, dark') + sor ('salt marsh, salt lake').

b_jilanjik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Zhylanshyk (Jilanjik / Dschilantschich) is documented only in modern Russian Imperial and Soviet cartography.
b_jilanjik.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Zhylanshyq (CK3: Jilanjik / Dschilantschich), from zhylan ('snake') + diminutive suffix -shyq, referring to a winding steppe stream.

current_repo_state.name: Dschilantschîch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dschilantschîch).

b_tuzdyn.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tuzdyn / Tuzdy is a Kazakh salt-lake/stream toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_tuzdyn.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Tuzdy (with genitive/cartographic variant Tuzdyn), from tuz ('salt') + -dy ('salty'), a generic descriptor for saline lakes and streams.

b_ulytau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Ulytau mountains are first attested in medieval Arabic/Persian geography in al-Idrisi (1154 CE, Nuzhat al-mushtaq) and Gardizi (11th century CE).
b_ulytau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Ulytau ('Great Mountain'), from uly ('great') + tau ('mountain'), designating the central Kazakh mountain range.

b_tamdins.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tamdy River in Ulytau (known for Bronze Age and medieval petroglyphs) has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_tamdins.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Tamdy (CK3 pluralized/Russianized key tamdins), a river and valley in the Ulytau region derived from tam + -dy.

b_jaman_arganaty.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Arganaty / Zhaman Arganaty range north of Ulytau is documented only in modern Russian/Kazakh cartography.

morphemes.translation: Arganaty (mountain range name, cf. Mongolic arghali / argan 'mountain sheep / ridge')

b_jaman_arganaty.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Zhaman Arghanaty, a qualifier compound contrasting with Zhaqsy Arghanaty ('Good Arganaty') in the Ulytau uplands.

b_chumkar_kia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Chumkar-Kia (Tschumkar-Kie) is a Kazakh steppe toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_chumkar_kia.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Shumqarqiya (Russian Chumkar-Kia), a compound of shumqar ('gyrfalcon') + qiya ('steep slope, cliff').

current_repo_state.name: Tschumkar-Kîe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tschumkar-Kîe).

b_tusum_kum.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tosyn Kum (Tusum-Kum) sands along the Turgay River are documented only in modern Russian/Kazakh cartography.
b_tusum_kum.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Tosyn qumy (Russian Tusum-Kum), an 820 sq km sandy tract along the Turgay River in Kostanay Region.

b_murun_tomis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Murun Tomis is a minor Kazakh steppe toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_murun_tomis.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound incorporating muryn ('nose, headland, promontory') + tomys (obscure local element).

current_repo_state.name: Murun Tomis
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Murun Tomis).

b_tatyr_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tatyr-Kul (Kazakh Tatyrköl) is a Kazakh lake toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_tatyr_kul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Tatyrköl (Russian Tatyr-Kul), from tatyr ('barren clay/salt pan') + köl ('lake').

b_tumar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tumar is a minor Kazakh steppe toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_tumar.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh tumar ('triangular protective amulet'), a cultural term borrowed into Turkic via Persian/Arabic ultimately from Greek tomarion.

current_repo_state.name: Tumar
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tumar).

b_tibis_sor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tibis-Sor is a Kazakh salt-flat toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_tibis_sor.etymology_analysis: Kazakh salt-flat toponym combining the local element tibis with sor ('salt marsh, alkali depression').

b_kyzyl_yar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kyzyl-Yar (Kazakh Qyzylzhar) is a generic Kazakh topographic name documented only in modern cartography.
b_kyzyl_yar.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Qyzylzhar (Russian Kyzyl-Yar), a common descriptive compound meaning 'red bluff/cliff', from qyzyl ('red') + zhar ('steep bank, bluff').

b_turgay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the settlement of Turgay (Torgai) was founded in 1845 CE as a Russian fortress on the Turgay River, which itself has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_turgay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Torghay (Russian Turgay), identical in form to Kazakh torghay ('lark, sparrow-like bird'), designating the 825 km river in central-northwestern Kazakhstan.

current_repo_state.name: Turgay
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Turgay).

b_jaman_akkul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Zhaman-Akkol (Jaman-Akkul) in Kostanay/Turgay is documented only in modern Russian/Soviet cartography.
b_jaman_akkul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Zhaman-Aqqöl (Russian Zhaman-Akkol), a qualifier compound meaning 'Lesser/Bad White Lake', contrasting with Zhaqsy-Aqqöl ('Good White Lake').

b_agairik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Agairik (Agairich) in the Altai/East Kazakhstan region is documented only in modern cartography.
b_agairik.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Altai Turkic compound Aghayryq ('white fork/branch'), from aq ('white') + ayryq ('fork, divide').

b_bostal.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Bostal River in the Altai region is documented only in modern Russian/Soviet cartography.
b_bostal.etymology_analysis: Altai/Turkic hydronym Bostal, likely from bos ('pale, grey, empty') + tal ('willow').

b_belesek.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Belesek is a minor Kazakh/Altai topographic name documented only in modern cartography.
b_belesek.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic topographic term derived from bel ('ridge, saddle, pass'), denoting a small pass or ridge.

b_narym_DZU.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while modern historians associate the Naryn/Narym basin with the Alat tribe in Chinese annals, the river name Narym/Naryn itself is not attested in written sources <= 867 CE.
b_narym_DZU.etymology_analysis: Russian Narym (Kazakh Naryn), a right tributary of the Irtysh in East Kazakhstan; often linked to Mongolic/Turkic naryn ('narrow, fine').

b_kurchum.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the village of Kurshim (Kurchum) was founded in 1914 CE, and the Kurshim River has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kurchum.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Kürshim (Russian Kurchum), a 280 km right tributary of the Irtysh in East Kazakhstan Region.

b_kurguni.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Kurguni' has no documented pre-867 attestation and appears to be a synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name.

morphemes.translation: unidentified or synthetic CK3 place name (unknown etymology)

b_kurguni.etymology_analysis: Unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the East Kazakhstan/Altai region without a clear attested Kazakh or Russian cartographic counterpart.

b_torangy_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Torangy-Kul (Kazakh Toranghyköl) is a Kazakh lake toponym documented only in modern cartography.
b_torangy_kul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Toranghyköl (Russian Torangykul), from toranghy ('desert/diversifolious poplar') + köl ('lake').

b_chaklym.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; modern/CK3 Dzungarian toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_chaklym.etymology_analysis: Likely a Turkic or Mongolic local toponym in the Altai-Dzungarian frontier; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_sarytau.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Turkic/Kazakh descriptive oronymic compound ('yellow mountain') not documented in pre-867 sources.

b_altay.first_mention_attestation: Modern city (originally Chenghua Temple, Qing era; renamed Altay in 1953, prefecture/district established 1921); the Altai mountain name is attested earlier, but the settlement is post-867.

morphemes.translation: gold mountain (from Turkic altun / Mongolic altan 'gold' + tay 'mountain')

b_altay.etymology_analysis: Named after the Altai Mountains (ultimately from Turkic/Mongolic 'gold mountain').

b_kulris.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; synthetic or obscure CK3 Altai-region toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_kulris.etymology_analysis: Obscure or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Altai region; no pre-867 written attestation.

b_kran_DZU.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE as a settlement; named after the Kran River (Kelan River) flowing through Altay.
b_kran_DZU.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kran River (Kelan River), a tributary of the Irtysh flowing through Altay City.

b_burqin.first_mention_attestation: Burqin County established in 1919 CE in Altay Prefecture, Xinjiang; named after the Burqin River.
b_burqin.etymology_analysis: Named after the Burqin River, a major tributary of the Irtysh in northern Xinjiang.

b_talta.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; modern/CK3 Altai-region toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_talta.etymology_analysis: Local Altai-region toponym possibly related to Turkic tal ('willow'); unattested before 867 CE.

b_irmengtau.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Turkic/Kazakh oronymic compound with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_irmengtau.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh mountain name ending in tau ('mountain'); unattested before 867 CE.

b_qinggil.first_mention_attestation: Qinggil (Qinghe) County established in 1941 CE in Altay Prefecture, Xinjiang; named after the Qinggil River.
b_qinggil.etymology_analysis: Named after the Qinggil River (Qinghe) in northeastern Altay Prefecture.

b_chungul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; local Mongolic/Turkic toponym in Altay/Qinggil with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_chungul.etymology_analysis: Local Altay-region toponym; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_zagan-gol.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic hydronymic compound ('white river') not documented as a settlement before 867 CE.

b_tengerge.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic toponym in northern Xinjiang with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_tengerge.etymology_analysis: Mongolic toponym in the Altai region; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_borultokay.first_mention_attestation: Burultokay (Fuhai) County established in 1921 CE in Altay Prefecture, Xinjiang; name attested in Qing-era geographical records.

b_beshbalik.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Beš Balïq in the Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions (713 CE) and as Tang Beiting Protectorate (702 CE).
b_beshbalik.etymology_analysis: From Old Turkic beš ('five') + balïq ('city/town'), literally 'Five Cities', corresponding to Tang Beiting.

current_repo_state.name: Beschbalich
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Beschbalich).

b_fukang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fukang County by the Qing dynasty in 1776 CE (meaning 'prosperous and healthy').
b_fukang.etymology_analysis: Qing-era Chinese administrative name fùkāng (阜康, 'prosperous and peaceful'), coined in 1776.

b_cheshi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Shiji (91 BCE) and Book of Han (111 CE) for the ancient kingdom of Cheshi (Gushi), active from c. 108 BCE.
b_cheshi.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (車師) of the ancient Indo-European (Tocharian/Saka) oasis state in the Turpan-Jimsar region.

b_beilu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, ch. 96B, 111 CE) as the Western Regions state of Beilu (卑陸) in northern Tianshan.
b_beilu.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (卑陸) in the Book of Han for a small pastoral-oasis polity in northern Dzungaria/Tianshan.

b_pilu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; appears to be a CK3 variant or corruption of Beilu (卑陸) or a local Dzungarian toponym.

morphemes.translation: variant of Beilu or local Dzungarian toponym

b_pilu.etymology_analysis: Likely a variant form of Han-era Beilu or a local toponym; not independently attested before 867 CE.

b_bugur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE under the Mongolic/Uyghur name Bügür/Bugur; the oasis was known as Luntai/Wulei in Han-Tang sources.
b_bugur.etymology_analysis: Mongolic/Uyghur name (Bügür/Bugur) for the Luntai oasis, replacing earlier Chinese Luntai/Wulei after 867 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: Han garrison at Luntai (101–80 BCE) and Protectorate seat at Wulei (60 BCE).

b_manas.first_mention_attestation: Named after the Manas River; Qing garrison/county established in the 18th century (1763 CE).
b_manas.etymology_analysis: Named after the Manas River in northern Xinjiang.

b_jimsar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE under the modern name Jimsar; the site is the ancient Tang city of Beiting/Tingzhou (640 CE) and Han Yulishi.
b_jimsar.etymology_analysis: Post-867 Uyghur/Mongolic name for the ancient oasis of Beiting/Beshbalik.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (111 CE) / Old Book of Tang (640 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Yulishi and Tang Tingzhou/Beiting Protectorate seat.

b_yizhi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu, 445 CE) as the pastoral state of Yizhi (移支) in the Barköl area during the Later Han.

morphemes.translation: Later Han pastoral polity in eastern Xinjiang

b_yizhi.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (移支) in the Book of the Later Han for a pastoral nomadic state in the Barköl region.

b_yangjibalik.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Yuan-era sources (13th–14th century, as Yangjibaliq 仰吉八里) for a settlement near Manas/Changji.
b_yangjibalik.etymology_analysis: From Turkic yangi ('new') + balïq ('city/town'), attested in Yuan-dynasty Chinese sources as 仰吉八里.

b_wutanzili.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, ch. 96B, 111 CE) as the Western Regions state of Wutanzili (烏貪訾離) in Dzungaria.
b_wutanzili.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (烏貪訾離) in the Book of Han for a small pastoral-oasis polity in northern Xinjiang.

b_wusu.first_mention_attestation: Qing-era garrison/settlement established in the 18th century (Kur Kara Usu); named after the Kara Usu ('black water') river.
b_wusu.etymology_analysis: Shortened Chinese form (Wūsū 烏蘇) of Mongolic Kur Kara Usu ('snowy black water' river).

b_hoboksar.first_mention_attestation: Hoboksar (Hefeng) County established in 1913 CE in Tacheng Prefecture, Xinjiang; named after the Hobok River/valley.
b_hoboksar.etymology_analysis: From Oirat Mongolic Qoboɣ Sayir, referring to the Hobok River and its gravelly valley.

b_tiebuken.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; modern/Qing-era toponym (Tiebuken-wulimukey, Hoboksar) with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_tiebuken.etymology_analysis: Modern Oirat/Chinese-transcribed toponym in Hoboksar; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_jie_DZU.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, ch. 96B, 111 CE) as the Western Regions state of Jie (劫國) in the eastern Tianshan.
b_jie_DZU.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (劫國) in the Book of Han for a small polity in the eastern Tianshan/Changji region.

b_sulugu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; local Dzungarian toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_sulugu.etymology_analysis: Local Dzungarian toponym; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_cheko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; local or CK3 Dzungarian toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_cheko.etymology_analysis: Local or synthetic CK3 toponym in Dzungaria; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_kaerji.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; modern/Qing-era Dzungarian toponym (cf. Kaerji/Qarji) with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_kaerji.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription of a Mongolic/Turkic local toponym in northern Xinjiang; unattested before 867 CE.

b_jeminay.first_mention_attestation: Jeminay County established in 1930 CE in Altay Prefecture, Xinjiang; name attested in Qing-era border records.
b_jeminay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Mongolic toponym in western Altay Prefecture; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_ulan_chuzir.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic descriptive toponym ('red salt marsh/soda flat') with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_ulan_chuzir.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic ulaan ('red') + khujir ('salt marsh/alkali flat').

b_bulun-tok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic/Turkic descriptive toponym (cf. Bulun-Tokhoy 'corner/bend') with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_bulun-tok.etymology_analysis: Related to Mongolic bulun ('corner/bay') + tokhoy ('riverbend'); unattested before 867 CE.

b_olon-bulak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic descriptive compound ('many springs') with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_olon-bulak.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic olon ('many') + bulag ('spring'); a common descriptive steppe toponym.

b_barkul.first_mention_attestation: Qing fortress/prefecture established at Barkol in 1731 CE; named after Barkol Lake (earlier Pulei in Han-Tang sources).
b_barkul.etymology_analysis: Named after Barkol Lake (Turkic köl 'lake'); replaced the earlier Han-Tang name Pulei.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient kingdom and lake of Pulei (蒲類) in Han and Tang sources.

b_liaotun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Chinese military-colony/station name (literally 'distant garrison') from Qing or later era.
b_liaotun.etymology_analysis: Chinese place name ending in tún ('garrison/settlement'); unattested before 867 CE.

b_pulei.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, 111 CE, describing Zhao Chongguo's 71 BCE campaign as General of Pulei 蒲類).

morphemes.translation: ancient name of Barkol Lake and polity

b_pulei.etymology_analysis: Han-era Chinese transcription (蒲類) for the Barkol basin and lake.

b_burgasutai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic descriptive toponym ('place with willows') with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_burgasutai.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic burgasu ('willow') + -tai ('having'), a common descriptive toponym.

current_repo_state.name: Burgasutai
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Burgasutai).

b_urtu_bulak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Mongolic descriptive compound ('long spring') with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_urtu_bulak.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic urt ('long') + bulag ('spring'); a generic descriptive steppe toponym.

b_hami.first_mention_attestation: Earliest verifiable attestation of Qămūl (Kumul/Chamil) is in Gardīzī's Zayn al-Akhbār (c. 1050 CE); earlier Han-Tang sources call the oasis Yiwu/Yizhou.
b_hami.etymology_analysis: From Uyghur Qumul / Qamil (rendered in Chinese as Hāmì 哈密 during the Ming); replaced Han-Tang Yiwu/Yizhou.

current_repo_state.name: Tschamil
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tschamil).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of the Later Han (73 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han military colony of Yiwu/Yiwulu (73 CE) and Tang prefecture of Yizhou (630 CE).

b_minggam.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; local eastern Xinjiang/Mongolic toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_minggam.etymology_analysis: Local Kumul/Hami-region toponym; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_chalamtum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; local or CK3 eastern Xinjiang toponym with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_chalamtum.etymology_analysis: Local or synthetic CK3 toponym in the Kumul/Hami region; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_kara_khoja.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation of the compound Kara-Khoja <= 867 CE; the name Qara-Khoja (Halahezhuo) is attested in Yuan- and Ming-era sources (13th-14th centuries CE).
b_kara_khoja.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old Uyghur qara ('black', 'great') and Qočo (Qocho), the Uyghur adaptation of Chinese Gaochang (高昌), attested as Halahezhuo (哈拉和卓) in Yuan and Ming sources.

current_repo_state.name: Karachoje
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Karachoje).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Chinese dynastic histories (Gaochang Commandery established by Former Liang in 327 CE; Tang prefecture of Xizhou established in 640 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Silk Road oasis city of Gaochang (高昌) was a major administrative center before 867 CE, becoming Tang Xizhou in 640 CE and the Uyghur capital Qocho in the mid-9th century.

b_yarkhoto.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Turkic-Mongolic name Yarkhoto (Yar-Khoto) is recorded in late-imperial and modern times for the ruined city of Jiaohe.
b_yarkhoto.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Turkic-Mongolic compound of Uyghur yar ('ravine, steep bank') and Mongolic khoto ('town, city'), referring to the cliff-top ruins of Jiaohe.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 111 CE) and Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu)
older_name_by_867.notes: Jiaohe (交河, 'river junction') was attested in Han dynastic histories as the capital of the Nearer Jushi (Cheshi) kingdom.

b_turpan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Khotanese tturpanä in the Dunhuang manuscript Shi Hexi Ji dated 925 CE; no written attestation of the name Turpan <= 867 CE.
b_turpan.etymology_analysis: First recorded in Khotanese as tturpanä (925 CE) and later in Yuan/Ming Chinese as Tulufan (吐魯番); its ultimate etymology is uncertain, possibly linked to a local Tocharian or Turkic designation for the basin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian, c. 91 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Turpan Basin was attested as Gushi/Jushi (Cheshi) in the Shiji (c. 91 BCE) and administered from Jiaohe and Gaochang/Xizhou prior to 867 CE.

b_yidu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Yidu reflects the Chinese transcription Yiduhu (亦都護, from Old Uyghur Idiqut) applied to the Gaochang site (Idiqut-Shahri) in post-867 Yuan and Ming sources.
b_yidu.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Uyghur Idiqut (ıduq qut, 'holy fortune/majesty'), the royal title of the Qocho Uyghur rulers, transcribed in Chinese as Yiduhu (亦都護) and truncated here to Yidu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Chinese dynastic histories (Gaochang Commandery established in 327 CE; Tang Xizhou in 640 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Idiqut-Shahri ('City of the Idiqut') is a later Uyghur name for the ancient city of Gaochang.

b_achit_nuur.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Achit Nuur is a freshwater lake in western Mongolia documented only in modern geographical records.
b_achit_nuur.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym from achit ('beneficent, virtuous') and nuur ('lake'). Note: current_repo_state.name 'Harhirae' reflects the county seat c_harhiraa rather than the barony Achit Nuur.

b_tsagan_shibetu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tsagan Shibetu (Tsagaan Shuvuut) is a mountain massif in western Mongolia and Tuva documented only in modern cartography.
b_tsagan_shibetu.etymology_analysis: Mongolic oronym combining tsagaan ('white') with shuvuut ('bird-rich') or shibetu ('fenced, palisaded'), rendered in Russian cartography as Tsagan-Shibetu.

b_turgen_uul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Türgen Uul is a mountain range in the Mongolian Altai documented only in modern geographical records.
b_turgen_uul.etymology_analysis: Mongolian oronym from türgen ('swift, fast', referring to its mountain streams) and uul ('mountain').

b_tsambagarau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tsambagarav is a glaciated mountain massif in western Mongolia documented only in modern geographical records.
b_tsambagarau.etymology_analysis: Mongolian sacred mountain name borrowed from Tibetan Tshangs-pa dkar-po ('White Brahma').

b_tal_tugal.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tal Tugal is a local microtoponym or CK3 barony name with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_tal_tugal.etymology_analysis: Mongolian compound of tal ('plain, steppe') and tugal ('calf').

b_munkh_khairkhan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mönkh Khairkhan is a mountain massif in the Mongolian Altai documented only in modern geographical records.
b_munkh_khairkhan.etymology_analysis: Mongolian honorific oronym combining mönkh ('eternal') and khairkhan ('gracious, sacred mountain').

b_balgun.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Balgun has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_balgun.etymology_analysis: Regional Mongolic/Turkic toponym of the Dzungarian Gobi borderlands.

b_chumy-su.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Chumy-Su has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_chumy-su.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym combining the stem Chumy with su ('water, river').

b_boro_burgasu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Boro Burgasu is a Mongolic toponym documented only in late-imperial and modern cartography.
b_boro_burgasu.etymology_analysis: Mongolic descriptive toponym from boro ('grey, brown') and burgasu/burgasun ('willow, brushwood').

b_suchatu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Suchatu has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_suchatu.etymology_analysis: Mongolic descriptive toponym derived from sukhai ('tamarisk') with the possessive suffix -tu ('having tamarisk').

b_alak-nor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Alak-Nor (Alag Nuur) is documented only in modern geographical records.
b_alak-nor.etymology_analysis: Mongolic hydronym from alag ('variegated, dappled') and nuur ('lake').

b_kabtag.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kabtag (Khavtag / Baitag) is a mountain massif in the Dzungarian Gobi documented only in late-imperial and modern records.
b_kabtag.etymology_analysis: Mongolic oronym from khavtag/kabtag ('flat, broad'), referring to the Baitag/Khavtag mountain massif.

b_sugi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sugi has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_sugi.etymology_analysis: Local Dzungarian microtoponym without documented pre-867 attestation.

b_kara-asirgan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kara-Asirgan has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_kara-asirgan.etymology_analysis: Turkic compound of qara ('black') and asirgan (likely 'crossing/pass' or 'stallion').

b_morin_tolochai.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Morin Tolochai has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_morin_tolochai.etymology_analysis: Mongolic descriptive toponym meaning 'horse head' (morin 'horse' + tologai 'head, hillock').

b_tegurik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tegurik has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_tegurik.etymology_analysis: Mongolic descriptive toponym from tegürik/tögrög ('round, circular').

b_aley.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Aley River is documented only in Russian-era records from the 18th century onward.
b_aley.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Ob basin in Altai Krai, likely of Samoyedic or pre-Russian Turkic origin.

b_poperech.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Poperechnaya is a Russian-language hydronym dating to post-17th-century Russian settlement in Altai.
b_poperech.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive hydronym from poperechny ('transverse, crossing').

b_charych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Charysh River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.

morphemes.translation: proper hydronym (linked to ethnonym Choros or Turkic çaras)

b_charych.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the upper Ob basin, corresponding to Altay Çaras-Suu or Çoros.

b_anyu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Anuy River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.
b_anyu.etymology_analysis: Altai hydronym of pre-Russian Samoyedic or substrate origin.

b_kondoma.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kondoma River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.
b_kondoma.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Tom/Ob basin in Kemerovo Oblast, from Shor Qondum.

b_sary_chumych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sary-Chumysh is documented only in modern geographical records.
b_sary_chumych.etymology_analysis: Turkic qualifier compound meaning 'Yellow Chumysh', naming a left tributary of the Chumysh River.

b_ojin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ojin has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_ojin.etymology_analysis: Local or synthetic toponym in the Kondoma/Altai region without pre-867 attestation.

b_korgon.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Korgon (Korgon Range and River) is documented only in modern geographical records.
b_korgon.etymology_analysis: Altai oronym and hydronym (Korgon Range), likely from Turkic qorğun/qorğan ('fortress, refuge') or qorğaşın ('lead').

b_korginia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Korginia is a synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name derived from Korgon.
b_korginia.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym formed from Korgon with a Latinized -ia suffix.

b_anuy.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Anuy River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.
b_anuy.etymology_analysis: Altai hydronym of pre-Russian Samoyedic or substrate origin.

b_khuiten.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Khüiten Peak is documented only in modern geographical records.
b_khuiten.etymology_analysis: Mongolian oronym meaning 'cold', the highest peak of Mongolia in the Tavan Bogd massif. Note: current_repo_state.name 'Tawan Bogt' reflects the county seat c_tavan_bogd rather than the barony Khüiten.

b_khoton.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Khoton Lake is documented only in modern geographical records.
b_khoton.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym for the alpine lake in Altai Tavan Bogd National Park.

b_dayan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Dayan Lake is documented only in modern geographical records.
b_dayan.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym for Dayan Nuur in Bayan-Ölgii Province.

b_terektai.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Terekta (Terektinsky Ridge) is documented only in post-medieval and modern records.
b_terektai.etymology_analysis: Altay Turkic toponym from terek ('poplar') and suffix -tü ('having poplars').

b_ongutai.first_mention_attestation: First attested / founded in 1626 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ongutai.etymology_analysis: From Oirat Mongolic onggir/üngkür ('cave, hollow') with possessive suffix -doi ('place with caves/hollows'), Altay Ongdoi.

b_katun.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Katun River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.

b_biia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Biya River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.
b_biia.etymology_analysis: From Altay Biy ('lord, master', paired with Katun 'lady') or an earlier Samoyedic root bi ('water').

b_chumych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Chumysh River is documented only in post-medieval Russian-era records.
b_chumych.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the upper Ob basin in Altai Krai and Kemerovo Oblast.

b_yeshil_chumych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Yeshil Chumysh has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_yeshil_chumych.etymology_analysis: Turkic qualifier compound meaning 'Green Chumysh', formed on the model of Kara-Chumysh and Sary-Chumysh.

b_kyin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kyin has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_kyin.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym from qıyın ('difficult, narrow'), common in Altai/Kazakhstan.

b_mus_tagh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mus Tagh is a generic Turkic mountain name documented only in modern geographical records.
b_mus_tagh.etymology_analysis: Generic Turkic descriptive compound meaning 'ice mountain' (muz 'ice' + tağ 'mountain').

b_bilbe.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bilbe has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_bilbe.etymology_analysis: Unattested local or synthetic CK3 toponym in the Salair/Altai region.

b_ob.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Russian chronicles (Novgorod First Chronicle) in 1364 CE when Novgorodians campaigned down the Ob River; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ob.etymology_analysis: Borrowed into Russian from Komi ob ('river') or a descendant of Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́p- ('water, river').

b_obchikanak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name in the Upper Ob basin.
b_obchikanak.etymology_analysis: Appears to be a synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name combining the Ob River name with an unverified Siberian element 'chikanak'. No corresponding settlement or hydronym is attested in historical sources <= 867 CE.

b_berd.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Berd River is documented in Russian Siberian cartography and records from the 17th–18th centuries (e.g., Berdsk ostrog founded in 1716).
b_berd.etymology_analysis: Named after the Berd River (Russian: Бердь), a right tributary of the Ob rising on the Salair Ridge. Linguist A. P. Dulzon derived the hydronym from Yeniseian (Ket) *berčik-ul* ('strong/rapid river'), though folk etymologies also link it to Turkic *berdi* ('given').

b_inia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Inya River is first recorded in 17th-century Russian Siberian documents (also attested as Uen).
b_inia.etymology_analysis: Named after the Inya River (Russian: Иня), a major right tributary of the Ob flowing through Kemerovo and Novosibirsk Oblasts. Toponymists (such as A. P. Dulzon) trace the root *in-* to a Yeniseian (Ket, Imbatsk dialect) substrate hydronym.

b_sorok.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1748 (or 1751) as the Russian peasant village of Sorokino on the Chumysh River; incorporated into the city of Zarinsk in 1979.
b_sorok.eponym_details: Named after Soroka, an 18th-century Russian peasant settler who founded the village in 1748/1751.
b_sorok.etymology_analysis: Represents the historical village of Sorokino (rendered 'Soroch (Sorok)' in CK3) in Altai Krai, founded in 1748/1751 by a Russian peasant named Soroka and merged into Zarinsk in 1979.

b_our.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Ur River is documented in modern Russian cartography and the State Water Register.
b_our.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ur River (Russian: Ур), a 102 km left tributary of the Inya River in Kemerovo Oblast on the slopes of the Salair Ridge. Likely derived from a Yeniseian (*ur/ul* 'water, river') or Turkic (*or/ur* 'trench, valley') root.

b_kara_chumych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kara-Chumysh River is documented in modern Russian cartography and the State Water Register.
b_kara_chumych.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kara-Chumysh River (Russian: Кара-Чумыш), one of the two headstreams forming the Chumysh River in Kemerovo Oblast. Combines Turkic *qara* ('black, dark') with the regional hydronym *Chumysh*.

b_torema.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Salair region.
b_torema.etymology_analysis: No real-world settlement or geographic feature named Torema or Toreme is attested in the Salair/Upper Ob region in historical or modern cartographic sources.

b_iaya.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Yaya River is documented in Russian Siberian records from the 17th–19th centuries.
b_iaya.etymology_analysis: Named after the Yaya River (Russian: Яя; Chulym Turkic: Я-Су), a 380 km left tributary of the Chulym in Kemerovo and Tomsk Oblasts. Derived either from Ob-Ugric (Mansi *ya* 'river') or Turkic *yay* ('summer, summer pasture').

b_kalym.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Salair region.
b_kalym.etymology_analysis: No documented settlement or major geographic feature named Kalym is attested in the Salair region; the form matches the Turkic common noun *qalym* ('bride-price').

b_betpa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Betpak-Dala is documented in 19th-century Russian and Kazakh geographical sources.
b_betpa.etymology_analysis: Truncated form of Betpak-Dala (Kazakh: Бетпақдала), the vast desert plateau between the Sarysu River, Chu River, and Lake Balkhash. Usually interpreted as Kazakh *betpaq* (from Persian *bad-bakht* 'unfortunate, wretched' or Turkic *batpaq* 'marshy') + *dala* ('plain, steppe').

b_bos-tau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh steppe toponym in the Betpak-Dala region.
b_bos-tau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponymic compound *boz* ('grey, feather-grass steppe') + *tau* ('mountain'), meaning 'grey mountain'. No specific settlement or major feature in Betpak-Dala is attested under this name <= 867 CE.

b_tokobay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh clan/personal-name toponym.
b_tokobay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh anthroponymic/clan-derived toponym (*Тоқобай*). No historical settlement or feature is attested under this name <= 867 CE.

b_bulat.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh personal/clan-name toponym in Saryarka.
b_bulat.etymology_analysis: Derived from Turkic/Kazakh *bolat* / *bulat* ('steel', borrowed from Persian *pulad*), widely used as a personal and clan name. No settlement in Saryarka is attested under this name <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Bulat
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Bulat).

b_asaybay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh personal/clan-name toponym.
b_asaybay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh anthroponymic toponym (*Асайбай*), formed from a personal name with the honorific *-bay*. No settlement is attested under this name <= 867 CE.

b_manaka.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Taldymanaka (Manaka) River in Ulytau Region is documented in modern Kazakh and Russian cartography.

morphemes.translation: river name (hydronym in the Sarysu basin)

b_manaka.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Manaka river system (Taldymanaka, Sulumanaka) in Zhanaarka District, Ulytau Region, a major tributary of the Sarysu River.

current_repo_state.name: Manake
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Manake).

b_kuntun_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh steppe lake name.
b_kuntun_kul.etymology_analysis: Compound ending in Kazakh *köl* ('lake', rendered *-kul* in Russianized cartography), with an unverified first element. No lake or settlement by this name is attested <= 867 CE.

b_targyl.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Targyl is documented in modern Kazakh regional toponymy of the Karaganda/northern Lake Balkhash area.

morphemes.translation: striped, brindle (also a local steppe plant)

b_targyl.etymology_analysis: Refers to Targyl (Kazakh: Тарғыл), a valley and hill tract on the northern shore of Lake Balkhash in Karaganda Region, named after local steppe vegetation or its striped/variegated terrain.

current_repo_state.name: Targyl
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Targyl).

b_baykara.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh personal/clan-name toponym.
b_baykara.etymology_analysis: Kazakh anthroponymic/clan-derived toponym (*Байқара*). No settlement is attested under this name <= 867 CE.

b_ak-taylak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Aktaylak is documented in modern Kazakh cartography (e.g., the Aktaylak River in Karaganda Region and Aktaylak village in Ulytau Region).
b_ak-taylak.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym *Aq-taylaq* ('white young camel'), attested as a river in the Northern Balkhash basin (Karkaraly/Aktogay Districts, Karaganda Region) and as a village in Ulytau Region.

b_mukhor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Mongolic-derived toponym in eastern Saryarka.
b_mukhor.etymology_analysis: Reflects Mongolic *mukhar/mukhor* ('blunt, dead-end', often applied to blind valleys or intermittent streams). No settlement or feature by this name is attested <= 867 CE.

b_arkat.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Arkat Mountains are documented from the 19th century in Russian and Kazakh sources.
b_arkat.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Arkat Mountains (Kazakh: Арқат тауы) and nearby Arkat village in Abai Region, northeastern Kazakhstan, noted by 19th-century explorers such as P. P. Semyonov-Tyan-Shansky and Ch. Valikhanov.

b_urta_tau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ortatau is a Kazakh topographic name ('middle mountain') not attested in <= 867 CE written sources.
b_urta_tau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh positional compound *orta* ('middle') + *tau* ('mountain'), meaning 'middle mountain'. Excluded from natural proper names as a positional/locator compound and unverified in this specific subrange.

b_degelen.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Degelen mountain massif is documented in 19th–20th century Russian and Kazakh cartography.
b_degelen.etymology_analysis: Named after the Degelen mountain massif (Kazakh: Дегелең) in the northeastern Kazakh Uplands (Abai Region), later site of the Semipalatinsk Test Site's underground nuclear testing complex.

b_dogolan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mount Dogalan (Doghalang) is documented in modern Kazakh and Russian cartography of eastern Saryarka.
b_dogolan.etymology_analysis: Refers to Mount Dogalan (Kazakh: Доғалаң, 957 m) in eastern Karkaraly District near the Abai Region border, derived from Kazakh/Mongolic *dogha* ('bow, arch').

b_jinghiz.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Chingiztau is named after Genghis Khan (1162–1227) and documented in post-Mongol and modern Kazakh/Russian sources.
b_jinghiz.eponym_details: Named after Genghis Khan (Chinggis Khan, c. 1162–1227), founder of the Mongol Empire.
b_jinghiz.etymology_analysis: Named after the Chingiztau mountain range (Kazakh: Шыңғыстау) in Abai Region, eastern Kazakhstan, which bears the name of Genghis Khan combined with Kazakh *tau* ('mountain').

b_aljan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh personal/clan-name toponym.
b_aljan.etymology_analysis: Kazakh anthroponymic toponym (*Әлжан*). No settlement or geographic feature by this name is attested <= 867 CE.

b_kandygatai.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kandygatai hills in Abai Region are documented in modern Kazakh and Russian cartography.
b_kandygatai.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Kandygatai hills (Kazakh: Қандығатай) in Zharma District, Abai Region, formed with the Mongolic possessive/toponymic suffix *-tai/-tay*.

b_altyn-kolekis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Chingiztau region.
b_altyn-kolekis.etymology_analysis: Contains Turkic/Kazakh *altyn* ('gold, golden') followed by an unverified element *kolekis* (possibly a garbled transcription of *köl* 'lake'). No such place is attested <= 867 CE.

b_tekar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Chingiztau region.
b_tekar.etymology_analysis: No real-world settlement or geographic feature named Tekar is attested in the Chingiztau/Saryarka region in historical or modern cartographic sources.

b_chulak-terek.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sholak-Terek (Chulak-Terek) is documented in modern Kazakh and Russian cartography of eastern Kazakhstan.
b_chulak-terek.etymology_analysis: Kazakh topographic name *Sholaq-Terek* ('short/stunted poplar'), attested as a lake and river name in Zharma District, Abai Region.

b_jasky_kart.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Zhaksy-Kart is documented in modern Kazakh toponymy of Karaganda Region.
b_jasky_kart.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponymic compound *Zhaqsy Qart* ('good elder/ridge', paired with *Zhamanqart* in Karaganda Region). Excluded from natural proper names as a qualifier compound (*zhaqsy* 'good').

b_ak_tasty.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Aktasty is documented in modern Kazakh cartography of Karaganda Region.
b_ak_tasty.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym *Aqtasty* ('having white stones/rocks'), attested as a mountain (573 m) and several settlements/rivers in Karaganda Region.

b_karabas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Karabas in Karaganda Region is documented in 19th–20th century Russian and Kazakh records.
b_karabas.etymology_analysis: Kazakh settlement and railway station name *Qarabas* ('black head/summit') in Abai District, Karaganda Region, developed in the 20th century alongside the Karaganda coal basin and Karlag transit camp.

b_sokur.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Sokur (Sokyr) River in Karaganda Region is documented in modern Kazakh and Russian cartography.

morphemes.translation: blind (a river without outlet or intermittent stream)

b_sokur.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sokur (Kazakh: Соқыр) River near Karaganda, from Kazakh *soqyr* ('blind'), a common hydronymic term for intermittent or closed-basin streams.

b_altyn_su.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Altynsu River (tributary of the Nura) is documented in modern Kazakh cartography.
b_altyn_su.etymology_analysis: Named after the Altynsu River (Kazakh: Алтынсу, 'golden water/river'), a left tributary of the Nura River in Karaganda Region.

b_ku_jeku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or synthetic CK3 barony name in Karaganda Region.
b_ku_jeku.etymology_analysis: Likely a synthetic or garbled CK3 compound combining Kazakh *Qu* (cf. Mount Ku in Karaganda Region) with an unverified element *jeku*. No such settlement is attested <= 867 CE.

b_juzbay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unverified or minor Kazakh personal/clan-name toponym.
b_juzbay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh anthroponymic toponym (*Жүзбай*). No settlement or geographic feature by this name is attested <= 867 CE.

b_uliuty.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; variant transcription of the Olenti (Ulenty) river name in Saryarka.
b_uliuty.etymology_analysis: County-seat variant of Kazakh *Öleñti* (cf. `b_ulenty` in the same county), derived from *öleñ* ('sedge') + *-ti*.

b_ulenty.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Olenti (Ulenty) River is documented in 19th–20th century Russian and Kazakh sources.
b_ulenty.etymology_analysis: Named after the Olenti River (Kazakh: Өлеңті), a 273 km river flowing through Akmola, Karaganda, and Pavlodar Regions into Lake Auliekol, named from the Kazakh word for sedge (*öleñ*).

b_bayan_aulska.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1826 by Siberian Cossacks as stanitsa Bayan-Aul (Bayan-Aulsk); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bayan_aulska.etymology_analysis: Represents the Russianized form of stanitsa Bayan-Aulsk (modern Bayanaul, Pavlodar Region), founded in 1826 at the foot of the Bayanaul Range. Usually derived from Mongolic/Turkic *bayan* ('rich, blessed') + Kazakh *awyl* ('village/camp').

b_karkaraly.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1824 as a Russian Cossack fortress and settlement (Karkaralinsk) at the foot of the Karkaraly Mountains; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_karkaraly.etymology_analysis: Town in Karaganda Region founded in 1824 as Karkaralinsk, named after the nearby Karkaraly Mountains, whose peaks resemble the *qarqara* (traditional Kazakh plumed headdress).

b_kent_KAZ.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kent Range and village in Karkaraly District are documented in modern Russian and Kazakh cartography (site of the 17th-century Kyzyl-Kent palace).
b_kent_KAZ.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kent Range (Kazakh: Кент тауы) in Karkaraly District, Karaganda Region, from the Central Asian Turkic/Iranian toponymic term *kent* ('town, settlement').

b_edrei.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mount Edirey (Edrei) and Edrei village in Karkaraly District are documented in modern Kazakh and Russian cartography.
b_edrei.etymology_analysis: Refers to Mount Edirey (Kazakh: Едірей, 893 m) and Edrei village in Karkaraly District, Karaganda Region, situated north of the Arkalyk and Myrzhyk ranges.

b_nurtay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to Mount Nurtai (1,172 m) in the Kyzyltas massif of Saryarka, documented in modern Kazakh/Russian cartography.
b_nurtay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh oronym Nurtai (Нұртай), a summit in the Kyzyltas range of Central Kazakhstan, combining nur ('light, radiance') with tay ('colt' or regional toponymic element).

b_kyzyl_ray.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bronze Age Begazy-Dandybai archaeological sites exist in the massif, but written records of the name date to the modern period.
b_kyzyl_ray.etymology_analysis: Kazakh oronym Qyzylarai (Қызыларай), referring to the Kyzylarai mountain massif in Karaganda Region, from qyzyl ('red') and aray ('glow, dawn, clearing'), describing the reddish granite slopes.

b_kara_urunkay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; minor steppe toponym or CK3 map entry without pre-867 documentary record.
b_kara_urunkay.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh compound toponym combining qara ('black, dark') with urunkay/orynqay, a steppe locality name.

b_uch_katyn.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ushkatyn (Uch-Katyn) in Central Kazakhstan is attested only in modern/Soviet-era geographical and geological records.
b_uch_katyn.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Üshqatyn (Үшқатын, Russianized as Uch-Katyn/Ushkatyn), literally 'three women/ladies', a common Central Asian steppe toponymic motif.

b_bol_agach.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe toponym or CK3 map entry without pre-867 documentary record.
b_bol_agach.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh compound from bol ('abundant') or bal ('honey') and ağaş ('tree, grove'), denoting a wooded tract in the steppe.

b_tulkulam.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; note that current_repo_state.name ('Aigun') reflects the county seat c_aigun rather than the barony Tulkulam.
b_tulkulam.etymology_analysis: Steppe toponym in northern/central Kazakhstan, likely incorporating Kazakh tülki ('fox') with a toponymic suffix or second element.

b_kyzyl_kusku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; minor steppe toponym or CK3 map entry without pre-867 documentary record.
b_kyzyl_kusku.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym beginning with qyzyl ('red'), paired with a second element kusku.

b_jiren_suat.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe watering-place toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_jiren_suat.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Jirensuat (Жиренсуат), combining jiren ('chestnut, reddish-brown') and suat ('watering place, ford').

b_kalmek-imel.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; ethnonymic compound referencing Kalmyks (Oirats), whose presence in the Kazakh steppe dates to the post-867 era.
b_kalmek-imel.etymology_analysis: Compound steppe toponym combining the ethnonym Qalmaq ('Kalmyk') with emel/imel ('saddle, pass').

b_jorga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern/Soviet-era village and steppe toponym (Zhorga) in eastern Kazakhstan.
b_jorga.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Jorğa (Жорға), literally 'ambler' (a horse with a smooth pacing gait).

b_kokchetau.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1824 as a Russian military fortress (Kokchetav); named after Mount Kokshe / the Kokshetau massif, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kokchetau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh oronym Kökşetau (Көкшетау, Russianized as Kokchetav), meaning 'bluish mountain', from kökşe ('bluish') + tau ('mountain').

b_koy-bagar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Koybagar in Kostanay Region is documented only in modern Russian/Kazakh cartography.
b_koy-bagar.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Qoybağar (Қойбағар), meaning 'sheep-herding [lake/place]', from qoy ('sheep') + bağar ('tending').

b_akcha-adyr.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe hill toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_akcha-adyr.etymology_analysis: Kazakh descriptive toponym Aqşa-Adyr, from aqşa ('whitish') + adyr ('hill, ridge').

b_jildi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_jildi.etymology_analysis: Kazakh descriptive toponym Jeldi/Jildi ('windy'), from jel ('wind') + possessive/adjectival suffix -di.

b_bakanas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while medieval settlements in the Ili–Bakanas delta date to the 9th–13th centuries, the toponym Bakanas has no pre-867 written attestation. Note that current_repo_state.name ('Kulan-Uynach') reflects the county c_kulan_uynak.
b_bakanas.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Baqanas (Бақанас), denoting a dry river channel or seasonal river in eastern and southeastern Kazakhstan.

b_serek.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_serek.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Serek, from serek ('sparse, scattered'), likely referring to sparse vegetation or scattered springs/hills.

b_akjeku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe toponym or CK3 map entry without pre-867 documentary record.
b_akjeku.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym combining aq ('white') with jeke/jeku ('single, isolated').

b_barnaul.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Russian records in 1724 and officially founded in 1730 by Akinfiy Demidov at the confluence of the Barnaulka and Ob rivers.
b_barnaul.etymology_analysis: Named after the Barnaulka river (originally Barnaul); commonly derived from Teleut/Turkic *Boro-na-ul ('wolf river') or related Siberian hydronymic roots.

b_kasmala.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; river and village in Altai Krai documented only from the Russian colonization period (18th century onward).

morphemes.translation: river name in the Ob basin

b_kasmala.etymology_analysis: Hydronym Kasmala (Касмала), a left tributary of the Ob River in Altai Krai; likely of Turkic or pre-Turkic Siberian substrate origin.

b_barnaii.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; CK3 map variant or rendering of the Barnaulka/Barnay river area in Altai Krai.
b_barnaii.etymology_analysis: CK3 variant form associated with the Barnaulka river / Barnaul locality in Altai Krai.

b_gorkoalei.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian-era compound toponym in the Aley river / Kulunda steppe region.
b_gorkoalei.etymology_analysis: Russian-era qualifier compound combining gor'ko- ('bitter, saline') with the Aley River hydronym.

b_kachu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe toponym in the Kulunda / Ob–Irtysh interfluve without pre-867 documentary record.
b_kachu.etymology_analysis: Siberian/Kazakh steppe toponym (CK3 Katschû / Kachu) in the Kulunda steppe region.

b_dolons.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Dolon' (Kazakh Dölen) is a village in the Irtysh/Kulunda steppe attested only in modern times.
b_dolons.etymology_analysis: Steppe toponym Dolon' (Долонь, Kazakh Дөлен) in the Irtysh/Kulunda region.

b_molibay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_molibay.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym ending in -bay ('rich, noble'), likely from a personal or clan/locality name.

b_kuchuk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Kuchuk and Kuchuk settlements in Altai Krai are documented only from the Russian period (18th century onward).
b_kuchuk.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym Kuchuk (Кучук), meaning 'small' (contrasting with the larger Lake Kulunda immediately to the north), though folk tradition also links it to a post-867 ruler Kuchuk Khan.

b_lamych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; minor Siberian/Altai toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_lamych.etymology_analysis: Siberian Russian/regional toponym Lamych in the Kulunda steppe area.

b_kacharsku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian-era steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_kacharsku.etymology_analysis: Russianized adjectival settlement name (Kacharskoye / Kacharsku) built on a Turkic/steppe stem.

b_topolno.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian settlements named Topolnoye in Altai Krai were founded in the 18th century (e.g., 1737).
b_topolno.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive toponym Topolnoye (Топольное), derived from topol' ('poplar'), referring to poplar groves by lakes or rivers in Altai Krai.

b_kulunda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Kulunda and the Kulunda River are documented in the Russian period, while the village of Kulunda was founded in 1917.
b_kulunda.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh hydronym Qulyndy / Qulanda (Кулунда), meaning 'abounding in foals' or 'of wild asses (kulans)', giving its name to Lake Kulunda, the Kulunda River, and the Kulunda Steppe.

b_kuria.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian settlement of Kurya in Altai Krai was founded in the 18th century (c. 1759).
b_kuria.etymology_analysis: Russian dialectal geographic term kur'ya (курья), meaning 'oxbow lake' or 'river backwater', used as a village and tributary name in Altai Krai.

b_gorko.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian-era descriptive name for bitter/saline lakes in the Kulunda Steppe.
b_gorko.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive common-noun adjective Gor'koye ('bitter, brackish'), applied to numerous mineral lakes in the Kulunda Steppe.

b_dolgo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian-era descriptive name for elongated lakes in the Kulunda Steppe.
b_dolgo.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive adjective Dolgoye ('long'), applied to elongated lakes and settlements in the Kulunda Steppe.

b_kaska.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_kaska.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Qasqa (Қасқа), meaning 'bare, clear, or white-blazed' (commonly applied to bare hills or clearings in Saryarka).

b_junkur_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe lake toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_junkur_kul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh descriptive lake name Shūnqyrköl (Junkur-Kul), from şūnqyr ('hollow, depression') + köl ('lake').

b_chubar_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Shubarkol (Chubar-Kul) in Karaganda Region is documented in modern times (coal deposit discovered in 1983). Note that current_repo_state.name ('Chyzylteniz') reflects c_qyzylteniz.
b_chubar_kul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Şūbarköl (Шұбаркөл, Russianized as Chubar-Kul/Shubarkol), meaning 'mottled/speckled lake', from şūbar ('speckled') + köl ('lake').

b_konek.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_konek.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Könek (Көнек), literally 'leather milking-bucket', used metaphorically for a basin or well in the steppe.

b_jaksy_kyzy_kurt.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh compound toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_jaksy_kyzy_kurt.etymology_analysis: Kazakh qualifier compound beginning with jaqsy ('good') paired with kyzy-kurt (cf. Qazyğūrt).

b_karu_samys.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record. Note that current_repo_state.name ('Teniz') reflects the county c_teniz.
b_karu_samys.etymology_analysis: Kazakh steppe toponym, likely a variant or transcription of Qaraqamys ('black reeds') in the Lake Tengiz basin.

b_kokjetau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh oronymic name ('bluish mountain') in the Saryarka/Tengiz region without pre-867 documentary record.
b_kokjetau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh oronym Kökşetau ('bluish mountain'), from kökşe ('bluish') + tau ('mountain').

b_koja_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh lake toponym (Kozhakol) documented only in modern/19th-century records.
b_koja_kul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Qojaköl (Қожакөл), combining qoja ('khoja, master') with köl ('lake').

b_nura.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while medieval sites along the Nura–Ishim interfluve (such as Bozok) date archaeologically to the 9th–14th centuries, the earliest recorded topographical notes on the Nura River date to the 19th century (Ivan Shangin, 1816).

morphemes.translation: Nura (possibly from Mongolic/Turkic root for 'marsh, hollow' or 'cliff')

b_nura.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Nūra (Нұра), a major 978 km river of Central Kazakhstan flowing from the Kyzyltas mountains into Lake Tengiz.

b_kaptadyr.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record. Note that current_repo_state.name ('Togotai') reflects the county c_togotai.
b_kaptadyr.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym ending in adyr ('hill, ridge').

b_ajutasty.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe toponym without pre-867 documentary record.
b_ajutasty.etymology_analysis: Kazakh descriptive toponym Ayutasty (Аютасты), meaning 'having bear-rocks' or 'stony bear [place]', from ayu ('bear') + tas ('stone') + -ty.

b_arkalyk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1956 as a settlement for geologists and builders developing local bauxite deposits; granted city status in 1965. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_arkalyk.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Арқалық (Arqalyq), derived from arqa ('back, ridge, steppe upland') + -lyq ('pertaining to, place of').

b_bugaly.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Buguly (Bugaly) granite mountain massif in the Karkaraly-Kent range of central Kazakhstan.
b_bugaly.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Бұғылы (Būğyly), meaning 'abounding in deer/stags' (būğy 'deer' + -ly).

b_kulan_utmas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Kulanotpes (Kulan-Utmas) River flowing into Lake Tengiz in central Kazakhstan.
b_kulan_utmas.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Құланөтпес (Qūlanötpes), literally 'where the kulan (wild ass) cannot cross', referring to the river's deep or steep-banked channels.

b_sopak_sor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh steppe hydronym denoting an elongated salt marsh or lake (sor) in central Kazakhstan.

morphemes.translation: salt marsh, alkali flat, salt lake

b_sopak_sor.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Сопақсор (Sopaqsor), compounded from sopaq ('oval, oblong') + sor ('salt marsh, saline lake').

b_tokumbay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; reflects a Kazakh anthroponym/clan-derived toponym (Toqymbay) in central Kazakhstan.
b_tokumbay.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Тоқымбай (Toqymbay), a traditional personal/clan name formed from toqym ('saddlecloth') + bay ('rich, lord').

b_mautan_tas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh oronym/toponym in the Saryarka uplands.
b_mautan_tas.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym ending in tas ('stone, rock, rocky hill').

b_bazarka.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern village of Bazarga (formerly Bazarka) in Aksuat District, Abai Region, Kazakhstan.
b_bazarka.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Базарға / Russian Базарка (Bazarka), derived from bazar ('market', ultimately Persian bāzār).

b_kokpektinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1827 (some sources 1836) as the Cossack stanitsa Kokpektinskaya in eastern Kazakhstan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kokpektinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian-suffixed settlement form (Kokpektinsk / Kokpektinskaya) of Kazakh Көкпекті (Kökpekti), meaning 'abounding in saltbush/orache'.

b_guzkol.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to Guzkol Bay on the eastern shore of Lake Balkhash in Kazakhstan.

b_djusagach.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kazakh toponym (Jüzağaş / Dzhusagach) in the Balkhash-Alakol region.
b_djusagach.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Жүзағаш (Jüzağaş, Russianized Dzhusagach), literally 'hundred trees'.

b_ayagoz.first_mention_attestation: Modern city originated in 1931 as a Turkestan-Siberian Railway station settlement (incorporated 1939; nearby Russian fort Sergiopol founded 1831; 18th-century Chagatai manuscript also found in the area). No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ayagoz.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ayagoz River; interpreted either as Turkic ay + ögüz ('river of the Ay clan' / 'moon river') or folk-etymologized as 'beautiful eyes' (aya + köz).

b_kokpekty.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1827 (some sources 1836) as the Cossack stanitsa Kokpektinskaya on the Kokpekty River. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kokpekty.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Көкпекті (Kökpekti), meaning 'abounding in saltbush/orache', after the Kokpekty River.

b_urzhar.first_mention_attestation: Village founded by Siberian Cossacks in 1857 on the Urzhar River. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_urzhar.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Үржар (Ürjar), named after the Urzhar River, from ör/ür ('upper, steep') + jar ('ravine, steep river bank').

b_lepsink.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1846 as Lepsinsk near the headwaters of the Lepsy River; renamed Lepsy in 2010. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_lepsink.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement form Lepsinsk derived from the Lepsy River (Kazakh Лепсі).

b_sarkand.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1857 (Chokan Valikhanov / postal picket) and settled by Cossacks in 1858 on the Sarkand River. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sarkand.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Сарқант / Сарқан (Sarqant), named after the Sarkand River; often analyzed as sary ('yellow') + Sogdian/Iranian kand ('town') or a pre-modern river name.

b_usharal.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1871 (as stanitsa Stefanovskaya / Ucharal) on the Tentek River in Alakol District. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_usharal.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Үшарал (Üşaral), meaning 'three islands', referring to islands or braided channels in the Tentek River.

b_bole.first_mention_attestation: Bole County was established in 1920 (separated from Jinghe County) in Bortala, Xinjiang; attested in Qing/Dzungar era as Bortala. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bole.etymology_analysis: Chinese Bólè (博乐) is a phonetic abbreviation of Mongolian Bortala (Boro-Tala), meaning 'brown/gray steppe'.

b_ghulja.first_mention_attestation: Modern city (Ningyuan Fort) built by the Qing in 1762, succeeding the earlier Dzungar capital Khobak Sari established in the 17th century under Erdeni Batur. No written attestation of Ghulja <= 867 CE.
b_ghulja.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Ghulja / Kazakh Qulja derives from the Mongolian/Turkic word for the argali wild sheep (qulja); Chinese name Yining (伊宁) dates to 1914.

b_iren-chabirga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Eren Habirga (Iren-Chabirga) range of the eastern Tian Shan in Xinjiang.
b_iren-chabirga.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian Ereen Khavirga (Iren-Chabirga), literally 'variegated/mottled ribs', describing the striped mountain ridges.

b_avrautau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Avral-Ula (Awrau-tau / 阿吾拉勒山) mountain range in the Ili valley of Xinjiang.
