b_avrautau.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Mongolian-Turkic oronym combining Mongolian Avral (Avral-Ula) with Turkic tau ('mountain').

b_iliq.first_mention_attestation: The Ili River is attested in Chinese chronicles by 636 CE in the Book of Sui (Suishu) as Yili River (伊麗水), though the medieval town of Ilibalyk is archaeologically 9th–14th century and first attested in 13th-century sources. Audited as the settlement Iliq: no settlement attestation <= 867 CE.
b_iliq.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Ili River (Chinese Yīlì / 伊麗, Uyghur Ili), often linked to Turkic il / yal- ('shimmering') or an ancient Wusun/Turkic hydronym.

b_almaliq.first_mention_attestation: Medieval city in Huocheng County, Xinjiang; first attested in early 13th-century Mongol-era sources (c. 1211/1219, when its ruler Buzar submitted to Genghis Khan). No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_almaliq.etymology_analysis: From Turkic Almalyq, meaning 'place of apples' / 'apple orchard' (alma 'apple' + -lyq).

b_junzi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or minor CK3 barony name in the Ili valley of Xinjiang.
b_junzi.etymology_analysis: No documented pre-867 settlement corresponds to 'Junzi' in the Ili valley; appears to be a synthetic or late Chinese-transcribed CK3 barony name.

b_tekes.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Tekes River and Tekes County in Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang.
b_tekes.etymology_analysis: From Tekes (Текес), linked to Turkic/Mongolian teke ('ibex, mountain goat'), naming the main headwater river of the Ili.

b_kash.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Kash (Kax / 喀什河) River, a major tributary of the Ili River in Nilka County, Xinjiang.
b_kash.etymology_analysis: From Turkic qaš ('jade' or 'riverbank/ridge'), naming the Kash (Kax) River in the Ili basin.

b_musari.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; reflects Muzart (Muzat) Pass/River in the Tian Shan connecting the Ili valley with Aksu in Xinjiang.
b_musari.etymology_analysis: From Turkic Muz-art ('ice pass'), rendered in CK3 as Musari.

b_kunges.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Künes (Kunges) River, one of the two headwater tributaries forming the Ili River in Xinjiang.
b_kunges.etymology_analysis: From Uyghur/Kazakh Künes (Mongolian/Oirat Künges), meaning 'sunny' or 'sunlit valley'.

b_kalbin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Kalba Range (Kalbinsky Khrebet / Қалба жотасы) in East Kazakhstan.
b_kalbin.etymology_analysis: Russianized as Kalbinsky from Kalba (Kazakh Қалба), derived from Oirat/Mongolian kholboo ('link, connecting ridge').

b_ayrtau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to Mount Ayrtau (Айыртау) in Ulan District, East Kazakhstan Region (the nearby village of Ayrtau was called Zavidnoye until 2007).
b_ayrtau.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Айыртау (Ayırtau), literally 'forked mountain' (ayyr 'fork, saddle' + tau 'mountain').

b_ridder.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1786 after Russian officer Philip Ridder discovered gold, silver, and polymetallic ore deposits on May 31, 1786. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ridder.eponym_details: Named after Philip Ridder (1759–1838), a Russian mining officer who discovered rich gold, silver, and polymetallic ore deposits at the site on May 31, 1786.
b_ridder.etymology_analysis: Named after Russian explorer and mining officer Philip Ridder (1759–1838); known as Leninogorsk from 1941 to 2002.

b_bukhtarma.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 13th-century Mongol-era accounts of the 1208 Battle of the Irtysh/Buqdarma River between Genghis Khan and the Naiman-Merkit alliance. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bukhtarma.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Бұқтырма (Būqtyrma) / Middle Mongol Buqdarma, traditionally linked to Turkic buq- ('to hide, ambush') or an older Altai-Sayan substrate hydronym.

b_zyryan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1791 as Zyryanovsk after Gerasim Zyryanov discovered polymetallic ore deposits; renamed Altai in 2019. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_zyryan.eponym_details: Originally named Zyryanovsk (Zyryan) after Gerasim Zyryanov, an 18th-century Russian miner who discovered polymetallic ore deposits there in 1791.
b_zyryan.etymology_analysis: Named Zyryan (Zyryanovsk) after discoverer Gerasim Zyryanov (1791); renamed Altai in 2019 after the Altai Mountains.

b_sasyk_kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to Lake Sasykkol in the Alakol Depression of eastern Kazakhstan.

b_arkalyk_KAZe.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; represents an eastern Kazakhstan toponym/locality (Arkalyk) in the Sasykkol/Semey region.
b_arkalyk_KAZe.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Арқалық (Arqalyq), derived from arqa ('ridge, upland') + -lyq.

b_semey.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1718 as the Russian fortress of Semipalatinsk by decree of Peter the Great near seven ruined Buddhist temples; renamed Semey in 2007. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_semey.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Semey is adapted from Russian Semipalatinsk ('seven chambers/temples'), referring to seven Dzungar/Buddhist stone temples near the 1718 fort.

b_uba_KAZ.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Uba (Übi) River, a right tributary of the Irtysh in East Kazakhstan Region.
b_uba_KAZ.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Үбі (Übi) / Russian Uba, naming the 278-km tributary of the Irtysh River.

b_oskemen.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1720 as the Russian fortress of Ust-Kamennaya (later Ust-Kamenogorsk) at the confluence of the Irtysh and Ulba rivers. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Kazakh adaptation of Russian Ust-Kamenogorsk ('mouth of the stony mountains')

b_oskemen.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Өскемен (Öskemen) is a phonetic adaptation of Russian Ust-Kamenogorsk (ust' 'river mouth' + kamen' 'stone' + gora 'mountain').

b_balasaghun.first_mention_attestation: Although founded by Sogdians and occupied in the 9th century, Balasagun is first attested in written historical sources under 942–943 CE (Kara-Khanid conquest recorded by Muslim historians) and in the Hudud al-Alam (982 CE). No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_balasaghun.etymology_analysis: Also known in Turkic as Quz-Ordu; generally analyzed as Turkic/Sogdian bala ('city/town') + sagun (a Turkic official title).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (646 CE, describing his 629 CE visit)
older_name_by_867.notes: Suyab (Ak-Beshim, c. 15 km away in the Chüy Valley) was the main political and commercial center of the valley before being supplanted by Balasagun in the 10th–11th centuries.

b_narin.first_mention_attestation: Modern city of Naryn was established as a Russian fortress in 1868 on the Naryn River. No written attestation of Naryn <= 867 CE.
b_narin.etymology_analysis: Named after the Naryn River; variously derived from Mongolian narin ('narrow, slender') or Turkic/Mongolian naran ('sunny').

b_barskhan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 9th century by Ibn Khordadbeh in Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (first redaction c. 846 CE, also drawing on Tamim ibn Bahr's c. 821 CE journey) as Barskhan / Upper Nushajan.
b_barskhan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Barskhan (modern Kyrgyz Barskoon); C. E. Bosworth notes a traditional derivation from Persian Pārsi-khwān ('Persian-literate'), while folk etymology links it to Turkic bars ('snow leopard') + khan.

b_pishkek.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1825 as the Kokand Khanate fortress of Pishpek (later Frunze 1926–1991, now Bishkek). No written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: wooden churn/dasher used for making kumis

b_pishkek.etymology_analysis: Kyrgyz Bishkek (19th-century Pishpek) is traditionally derived from the Kyrgyz word for a kumis-churning dasher (bishkek) or a local folk hero's lost churn.

b_cherik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Cherik (Черик) Kyrgyz tribe of the Right Wing, primarily inhabiting At-Bashi District in Naryn Region.
b_cherik.etymology_analysis: From Old Turkic čerig ('army, warrior, troop'), the ethnonym of a major Kyrgyz Right Wing tribe.

b_tinimseyit.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Tynymseyit (Тынымсейит) Kyrgyz tribe of the Naryn/Issyk-Kul region.
b_tinimseyit.etymology_analysis: Kyrgyz tribal ethnonym Tynymseyit, compounded from tynym ('peace, rest') + seyit ('lord, sayyid').

b_bagish.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bagysh is a modern village in Jalal-Abad Region, Kyrgyzstan, and a Kyrgyz tribal ethnonym attested in 16th-century and later genealogies.

morphemes.translation: elk / moose (also a Kyrgyz tribal ethnonym)

b_bagish.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kyrgyz Bagysh tribe/clan (from Kyrgyz bagysh 'elk, moose'), which is attested in post-medieval Kyrgyz tribal genealogies (16th century onward) rather than pre-867 written sources.

b_suyab.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (compiled 646 CE) as the town of the Suye (Suyab) River, visited c. 629–630 CE.
b_suyab.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Iranian/Sogdian hydronym Suyab (Persian/Sogdian suy + ab 'water, river'), recorded in Chinese as Suye (碎葉) by Xuanzang (646 CE); also known as Ordukent, its ruins lie at Ak-Beshim near Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan.

b_nevaket.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Nawikat in al-Khwarizmi's Kitab Surat al-Ard (c. 833 CE) and later in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846–885 CE); earlier attested in Chinese calque as Xincheng ('New City') in Xuanzang (646 CE).
b_nevaket.etymology_analysis: Sogdian compound meaning 'New Town' (naw 'new' + kath 'town, city'), calqued into Tang Chinese as Xincheng (新城) and recorded in Arabic geographical works as Nawikat / Nawakath; archaeological ruins lie at Krasnaya Rechka in the Chüy Valley, Kyrgyzstan.

b_ashpara.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; medieval Aspara/Ashpara is attested in Timurid chronicles such as Nizamuddin Shami's Zafarnama (1404 CE) and Sharafuddin Ali Yazdi's Zafarnama (1425 CE).
b_ashpara.etymology_analysis: Medieval Silk Road town in the western Chüy Valley (ruins at Aspara/Asrantobe near the Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan border); its name is of uncertain Iranian or Turkic origin and first appears in Timurid-era written sources.

b_taraz.first_mention_attestation: First recorded under the name Talas in 568 CE by the Byzantine historian Menander Protector (embassy of Zemarchus to Istemi Qaghan), and later as Daluosi by Xuanzang (646 CE).
b_taraz.etymology_analysis: Named after the Talas River; attested as Talas in 568 CE Byzantine records, Daluosi in Tang Chinese, and Taraz in Islamic sources, with 1st-century BCE Xiongnu Zhizhi fortress remains nearby.

b_merke.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mirki in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (first draft c. 846 CE, revised 885 CE) and subsequently by Qudama ibn Ja'far and al-Maqdisi.

morphemes.translation: place of healing / center (uncertain pre-Kazakh origin)

b_merke.etymology_analysis: One of the few settlements in Zhetysu to retain its early medieval name (Mirki in 9th-century Arabic itineraries), located in Jambyl Region, Kazakhstan near the Turkic Sanctuary of Merke.

b_sayaq.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sayak is a Kyrgyz tribal ethnonym attested in post-medieval genealogies (16th–19th centuries) and a 20th-century Kazakh settlement name.

morphemes.translation: solitary / wanderer (also a Kyrgyz tribal name)

b_sayaq.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to the Kyrgyz Sayak tribal name (Turkic sayak 'solitary, wanderer') or modern Kazakh Sayak; neither is attested as a settlement <= 867 CE.

b_ebi-nor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Mongolic/Oirat hydronym Ebi-Nor (Lake Ebinur / Aibi Lake) is attested from the post-Mongol/Qing era.
b_ebi-nor.etymology_analysis: Mongolic/Oirat hydronym for Xinjiang's largest salt lake (Ebi Lake / Aibi Hu), combining ebi with nuur ('lake').

b_dahyansi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Daheyanzi (大河沿子) is a modern Chinese-named town in Jinghe County, Xinjiang.
b_dahyansi.etymology_analysis: Transliteration of Mandarin Chinese Daheyanzi (大河沿子, 'big river bank'), a modern town in Jinghe County near Ebi Lake.

b_emil.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Emil River and Yelü Dashi's 1130 CE base there are first recorded in the History of Liao (Liao Shi, compiled 1344 CE) and 13th-century Mongol-era histories.
b_emil.etymology_analysis: Named after the Emil (Emin) River flowing from Xinjiang into Lake Alakol; Yelü Dashi established his first western base on the Emil in 1130 CE.

b_sarychulsyn.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sarychulsyn is a synthetic CK3 barony name with no identified historical settlement.
b_sarychulsyn.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym resembling Turkic sary ('yellow') paired with an unattested second element.

b_ala-kul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation of the name Ala-Kul / Alakol <= 867 CE; the lake is described in 13th-century travelogues (William of Rubruck, 1253 CE) and later Timurid sources.
b_ala-kul.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh hydronym meaning 'variegated lake' (ala 'variegated, dappled' + köl 'lake'), referring to Lake Alakol in east-central Kazakhstan.

b_modo-bartik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Modo-Bartik is a synthetic CK3 barony name with no identified historical settlement.
b_modo-bartik.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name in the Tarbagatai/Emil region without documented historical or modern settlement attestation.

b_jinsko.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Jinghe (精河) is a Qing-era and modern county/town in Bortala, Xinjiang, named after the Jing River.
b_jinsko.etymology_analysis: Derived from Mandarin Chinese Jinghe (精河, 'clear river'), rendered in CK3 via a Russian/dialectal form Jinsko.

b_kuytun.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kuytun River is first attested as Kuiteng (奎騰) in the History of Yuan (Yuan Shi, compiled 1370 CE), and the modern city was established in 1975.
b_kuytun.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic küiten ('cold'), originally referring to the Kuytun River in northern Xinjiang and recorded in Chinese in the 14th-century Yuan Shi.

b_koltun.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Koltun is a synthetic CK3 barony name with no identified historical settlement in Xinjiang.
b_koltun.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name in c_jinsko, possibly an altered doublet of Kuytun or an invented steppe-style name.

b_karamay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Karamay was founded as an oil-producing city following the discovery of the Karamay oil field in 1955.
b_karamay.etymology_analysis: From Uyghur qara may ('black oil'), referring to natural bitumen/oil seeps near the modern city established in 1955.

b_baiyang.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Baiyang (白杨) is a modern Chinese name for the Baiyang River and a 21st-century city in Xinjiang.
b_baiyang.etymology_analysis: Mandarin Chinese Baiyang ('white poplar'), referring to the Baiyang River in northern Xinjiang near Karamay.

b_toli.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Toli County in Tacheng Prefecture, Xinjiang, is a Qing/20th-century administrative locality.
b_toli.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic/Oirat toli ('mirror'), used as the name of Toli County in northern Xinjiang.

b_aksuyek.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Aksuyek is a modern village in Moiynkum District, Jambyl Region, Kazakhstan, named after the Aksuyek River.
b_aksuyek.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound aq süyek ('white bone', also a term for Kazakh nobility), applied to the Aksuyek River rising in the Khantau massif and the nearby Soviet-era settlement.

current_repo_state.name: Aksuyech
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Aksuyech).

b_shyganak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Shyganak is a modern village in Moiynkum District, Jambyl Region, Kazakhstan.
b_shyganak.etymology_analysis: Generic Kazakh topographic term shyghanaq ('bay, inlet'), designating a modern settlement near Lake Balkhash in Jambyl Region.

b_mirnyy.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mirny (Mirnyy) is a 20th-century Soviet-era mining town in Moiynkum District, Jambyl Region, Kazakhstan.
b_mirnyy.etymology_analysis: Russian adjective mirnyy ('peaceful'), a typical Soviet-era settlement name in Moiynkum District, Kazakhstan.

b_almaty.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Almatu is first attested on 13th-century coins and in the 16th-century Baburnama, though archaeological settlements in the area date earlier.
b_almaty.etymology_analysis: Derived from medieval Almatu / Almatau ('abounding in apples', from Turkic alma 'apple'), referring to the wild apple forests of the Trans-Ili Alatau foothills.

current_repo_state.name: Almaty
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Almaty).

b_talgar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the medieval precursor Talkhiz is first mentioned in the 10th-century Hudud al-Alam (982 CE), and the modern town was founded in 1858 as Stanitsa Sofiiskaya.
b_talgar.etymology_analysis: Modified from the medieval Silk Road settlement name Talkhiz (attested 982 CE, containing Iranian -gar 'mountain'); modern Talgar began as a Russian Cossack stanitsa in 1858.

b_kyzyl_suu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kyzyl-Suu is a common modern Turkic/Kyrgyz toponym (e.g., Kyzyl-Suu in Issyk-Kul Region, Kyrgyzstan).
b_kyzyl_suu.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Turkic/Kyrgyz compound meaning 'red water / red river', widespread across Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan.

b_kegen.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kegen is a modern rural locality and administrative center in Almaty Region, Kazakhstan.
b_kegen.etymology_analysis: Modern settlement in southeastern Almaty Region near the Kyrgyz border; its name is of uncertain Kazakh or Mongolic origin and lacks pre-867 documentation.

b_kaskelen.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; founded in 1857 as the Russian Cossack village Lyubavinskaya and later renamed after the Kaskelen River.
b_kaskelen.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kaskelen River in Almaty Region; the town originated as a 19th-century Cossack stanitsa (1857).

current_repo_state.name: Kaskelen
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kaskelen).

b_chu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for the settlement; Shu (formerly Chu) was founded in 1928 during construction of the Turkestan-Siberia railway and named after the Chu (Shu) River.

morphemes.translation: hydronym of uncertain pre-Turkic or Turkic origin

b_chu.etymology_analysis: Named after the Chu (Kazakh Shu) River; the modern railway town was established in 1928.

b_kurdai.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Korday (Kurdai) is a modern village and district center in Jambyl Region, Kazakhstan.

morphemes.translation: toponym of uncertain origin (associated with a local clan/hero name)

b_kurdai.etymology_analysis: Modern settlement and mountain pass name in Jambyl Region, Kazakhstan, lacking pre-867 written attestation.

b_kopathal.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kopathal appears to be a modern or CK3-adapted Kazakh compound (kopa + tal) with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_kopathal.etymology_analysis: Kazakh-type compound of kopa ('marshy lake / sedge-overgrown depression') and tal ('willow'), unattested in pre-867 written sources.

current_repo_state.name: Kopathal
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kopathal).

b_akzhar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Akzhar is a widespread modern Kazakh toponym for settlements and salt lakes.
b_akzhar.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Kazakh compound meaning 'white cliff / white bank' (aq 'white' + zhar 'cliff, ravine').

b_tamgaly.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while the petroglyphs date from the Bronze Age onward, the Kazakh name Tamgaly (Tanbaly) is post-867 CE and the site was documented in 1957.
b_tamgaly.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym meaning 'marked place / place with tamgas (carvings)', referring to the Bronze Age and later petroglyphs in the Chu-Ili Mountains.

b_qayaliq.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; medieval Kayalyk (Qayaliq, Antonovka site) is attested in 11th–13th century sources and famously described by William of Rubruck in 1253 CE as Cailac.
b_qayaliq.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym meaning 'rocky place' (qaya 'rock' + -lyq), the medieval capital of the Karluk yabghus in Zhetysu (modern Antonovka archaeological site).

b_ichiwooq.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ichiwooq appears in modern historical-atlas reconstructions of the 11th-century Karakhanid Khanate (e.g., Tan Qixiang's Historical Atlas of China).
b_ichiwooq.etymology_analysis: Karakhanid-period settlement name from modern historical cartography of Zhetysu; unattested in pre-867 written sources.

b_altyn-emel.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the name Altyn-Emel ('Golden Saddle') is associated with post-13th-century Mongol-era tradition and modern Altyn-Emel National Park.
b_altyn-emel.etymology_analysis: Turko-Mongolic oronym meaning 'golden saddle' (altyn 'golden' + emel 'saddle, mountain pass'), naming a pass and ridge in Jetisu Region, Kazakhstan.

b_uchkul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Uchkul is a generic Turkic toponym ('three lakes') not documented in Zhetysu prior to 867 CE.
b_uchkul.etymology_analysis: Generic Turkic compound meaning 'three lakes' (üch 'three' + köl 'lake').

b_taldiqorgan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; founded in 1869 as the Cossack village of Gavrilovka and renamed Taldy-Kurgan in 1920–1921.
b_taldiqorgan.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound taldy qorghan ('willow-lined fortress/mound'), applied to the 1869 settlement of Gavrilovka in the 1920s.

b_kopal.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Qapal (Kopal) was founded in 1847 as a Russian fortress on the Qapal River.
b_kopal.etymology_analysis: Named after the Qapal River in Jetisu Region, Kazakhstan; the settlement began as a Russian fort in 1847.

b_lyukum.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lyukum is a synthetic CK3 barony name with no identified historical settlement in Zhetysu.
b_lyukum.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name in c_uchkul without documented historical or modern settlement correspondence.

b_chuguchak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Chuguchak (modern Tacheng) emerged as a Qing-era commercial and garrison town in the 18th–19th centuries.
b_chuguchak.etymology_analysis: Historical Russian/European name (Chuguchak) for Tacheng (Uyghur Chöchek, Kazakh Shäweshek) in northern Xinjiang, a Qing-era frontier trade hub.

b_cherga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Cherga is a modern rural locality in Shebalinsky District, Altai Republic, Russia.
b_cherga.etymology_analysis: Modern Altai Republic village name (Altay Chargy), placed in c_chuguchak in CK3 without pre-867 written attestation.

b_zatsan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Zatsan is a synthetic CK3 barony name (possibly altered from Zaisan) with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_zatsan.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name in c_chuguchak, possibly a corruption of Mongolic zaisan ('noble / elder', as in Lake Zaysan).
